description_en: Located downstream from Nābhisthān (DLK0150 and DLK0151), on the left bank of the Nabhi River and 60 meters from its confluence with the Chhamghate, the site of Sīrasthān includes a still-active flame temple.The temple is part of an area know as Pañcakośī. The sites of the Pañcakośī are visited by pilgrims from all over western Nepal. The sites are notorious for their flame temples (natural gas flames), said to mark places where Satī's body parts fell while Śiva carried her charred body (Lecomte-Tilouine 2009). Sīrasthān is the place where Satī's head (sirā) fell.As at Nābhisthān (DLk0150 and DLK0151), this building and all those around it are of more or less recent construction. The Flame Temple (Jvālā Mandira) is oriented to the south, towards the Nabhi Khola. It has been remodelled in recent decades. A photograph by M. Gaborieau taken in 1967 shows that the northern façade was cracked and that the structure was leaning towards the west. The stone wall has plinths similar to those of the Temple of the Flame at Pādukāsthān (DLK0270). A newar-style tile roof runs around the temple, with a square stone lantern emerging in the centre, also covered by a four-sided tile roof.The stone door frame must be from an earlier period. The central part of the lintel has a Gaṇeśa framed by two pillars. The moulding of the lintel forms a projection above the head of the god.Inside, almost in line with the door, is the natural flame, housed in a small niche on the north wall. To the right of the flame, a unique historiated stele depicts a male figure seated on a throne with elaborate feet (DLK0150-001). In front of the figure, to his right, stands a very similar individual but half as tall as the first. He is also sitting on a chair and his two hands are making the sign of greeting (añjalimudrā). The top of the stele is triangular. The statue has been identified as a representation of a king (Sharma 2012, p. 67) although it is localy considered to represent a guru (Andolfatto 2019, p. 174) or Śiva and Pārvatī. The object may be dated from c. 14th-15th century.During his visit to the site in 1967, Marc Gaborieau was able to photograph several sculptures that have now disappeared (stolen or kept secret for fear of theft). Among these objects, some of which have been published in Prayag Raj Sharma's book, are a small stone sculpture of the Buddha, three repoussé metal sculptures and a stone stele of the Śiva-Pārvatī couple.

historical_events.event_description: Ancient inscription carved on the entablement of the temple, to the right above the door.Yogi Naraharinath mentions an inscription of Udhyot Chand dated of ŚS 1313 (1391 CE) (Naraharinath 1956, p. 208, cited inSharma 2012, p. 67). It is currently unclear whether this is the inscription in question.
